personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Dumbledore's personality is multi-layered and deliberately paradoxical. His dominant public traits — warmth, wit, gnomic humor, and apparently serene wisdom — are established through others' tributes (Doge's obituary, Harry's recollections) and through his own dialogue in the Pensieve memories: calm, deliberate, often ironic speech, with a habit of turning questions back on the asker. But the books crucially complicate this persona with a private self that is deeply flawed: vain, ambitious, self-reproaching, and capable of great cruelty through omission. In the King's Cross chapter, Dumbledore speaks with raw vulnerability — he describes himself as selfish, gifted, wanting to 'shine,' and haunted by guilt over Ariana. He weeps, he asks Harry's forgiveness, and he admits his obsession with the Hallows was a 'desperate man's dream.' His voice in this chapter is unlike any other in the series: direct, confessional, stripped of his usual deflecting wit. In the Pensieve sequences with Snape, his tone is cold and calculating when necessary ('If she means so much to you, surely Lord Voldemort would spare her?'), but also privately warm and even sardonic ('Keep an eye on Quirrell'). The books also show him managing others strategically — hiding information, orchestrating outcomes — while projecting calm. His humor is dry and self-aware even at the edge of death ('I daresay the moment will present itself in due course').
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve Dumbledore's surface personality reasonably well in the Pensieve scenes and the King's Cross sequence. His calm deliberateness with Snape is intact: 'That wasn't my intention,' 'Stand up, Severus,' 'If she means so much to you.' The King's Cross scene retains his warmth toward Harry ('You wonderful boy. You brave, brave man'), his humor about King's Cross being 'your party,' his philosophical cadences, and crucially his admission about the Deathly Hallows: 'I didn't trust you... I feared you would make the same mistake I made.' His self-deprecating regret is present, though abbreviated. The film's version of the scene also preserves key lines — 'Do not pity the dead, Harry. Pity the living' — and the characteristic habit of turning Harry's questions around. However, the film King's Cross scene is substantially compressed relative to the book. The extended confessional passages where Dumbledore describes his youth — his resentment, his vanity, his desire to escape, his complicity in Grindelwald's ideology, his grief over Ariana — are reduced to brief references. The film Dumbledore says he 'paid with his life' for taking the Stone and admits he didn't trust Harry, but the deep psychological excavation of the book version — where Dumbledore describes himself as 'selfish, more selfish than you... could possibly imagine,' and where he weeps in earnest — is truncated. Additionally, the film Snape memories are substantially cut from the books: the scene in which Dumbledore refuses to tell Snape why he needs Harry to have the sword, the scene where Dumbledore and Snape walk the grounds and Dumbledore invites Snape to his office ('Come to my office tonight... you shall not complain that I have no confidence in you'), and the scene in which Dumbledore explicitly describes his plan to let the wand's power die with him, are all absent. These scenes show a Dumbledore who is strategically withholding, calculating, and willing to use even his most trusted ally instrumentally — personality dimensions that the film only partially conveys.
personality_voice.difference: The core personality — warm, ironic, strategically wise, privately guilty — is preserved in both the King's Cross and Pensieve sequences. The film captures his voice adequately in dialogue. What is missing is the full interior portrait the books build: the confessional self-portrait of a vain young man who wanted glory, the extended admission of his failure to act against Grindelwald out of fear, and the precise texture of his relationship with Snape as a manager who reveals only what is necessary. The film Dumbledore is recognizable but slightly more uniformly sage-like and less exposed as an operator who uses people — including those he loves — for ends they only partly understand.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main personality traits and voice patterns are preserved — the wit, the warmth, the philosophical register, the guilt, the willingness to admit error. The penalty is for the loss of the most self-exposing passages in King's Cross and the strategic-withholding dimension visible in the full Snape memory sequence. These are not trivial: they are what separates book Dumbledore from a merely noble mentor figure. The simplification is real but does not fundamentally misrepresent him; it flattens the depth without reversing the characterization. Score: 18 (main personality preserved, but meaningful simplification of secondary traits and internal contradictions).

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Dumbledore's narrative role in Deathly Hallows is structurally central even in death. He functions as the absent architect of the entire plot: every major discovery (Horcruxes, their locations, the sword's purpose, the Hallows, Harry's true nature as a Horcrux, Snape's loyalty) traces back to plans Dumbledore set in motion before his death. His agency is exercised posthumously through: (1) the will (Deluminator, Snitch, Tales of Beedle the Bard), each item carrying a hidden purpose; (2) the Pensieve memories, which reveal the full plan to Snape and ultimately to Harry; (3) the instructions left with Snape (plant decoys for the Seven Potters, deliver the sword via the doe, tell Harry the truth at the right moment); (4) the King's Cross scene, where he directly explains the metaphysics of Harry's survival, the Hallows, and his own failures; (5) his portrait, through which he continues to communicate with Snape during the war. Beyond this posthumous agency, the books also show him as an active agent in the Pensieve: he recruits Snape, he engineers Draco's situation to protect the boy's soul, he plans his own death to neutralize the Elder Wand, he reasons about Harry's Horcrux status. His decisions shape the entire war. In the book's King's Cross chapter, he explains these decisions in detail, including admitting where his plan went wrong (he expected the wand's power to die with him; it didn't because Draco had already disarmed him).
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve Dumbledore's role as posthumous architect: the will scene is faithfully rendered, the Pensieve memories establish his plan with Snape, and the King's Cross scene preserves the key revelations (Harry as Horcrux, the Hallows, Harry's choice). The doe-and-sword subplot is present in the film though not explicitly resolved in Harry's dialogue with Dumbledore the way the book handles it. The portrait's role — through which Dumbledore communicates with Snape — is referenced when Harry enters the headmaster's office and finds the frames empty, but the portrait of Dumbledore giving active instructions to Snape (as shown in the book's Pensieve) is present in the Pensieve memory that shows the portrait saying 'Good. Very good! Now, Severus, the sword! Do not forget that it must be taken under conditions of need and valor.' This scene is absent from the film's Pensieve sequence. The film Pensieve reduces the Snape memories significantly: the scene where Dumbledore's portrait instructs Snape on how to deliver the sword, the extended scene where Dumbledore reveals Harry must die, and several intermediate scenes are cut or compressed. Crucially, in the film the scene where Dumbledore explains his plan to arrange his death so the wand's power dies with him is present but abbreviated: it covers the essentials (Draco must not kill him, Snape must do it) but omits the reasoning about Elder Wand succession that the book version elaborates. In King's Cross, the film preserves Dumbledore's key explanatory agency: he tells Harry about the Horcrux, he explains the Hallows mistake, he confirms Harry's choice. One significant transfer occurs: in the film, Harry explains the Elder Wand's true master to Voldemort during the final confrontation in the Great Hall, and the reasoning ('Draco disarmed Dumbledore... I disarmed Draco') is rendered fully. In the books, Harry also explains this, but the film compresses the preceding Pensieve material, meaning Harry's understanding is partly the audience's inference rather than fully grounded in shown Dumbledore-Snape scenes. The agency itself is not transferred to another character — it remains Dumbledore's — but the visibility of that agency is reduced.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Dumbledore's narrative function as posthumous architect is preserved. The will, the Pensieve, the King's Cross scene, and the doe-sword subplot all remain. What is reduced: the portrait's active role in directing Snape, the full elaboration of the wand succession plan, and several intermediate Pensieve moments that show Dumbledore actively managing Snape over years. These are reductions in the display of his agency rather than transfers of that agency to another character.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The core narrative role is intact. The reduction is real but does not reassign his functions. The missing portrait scenes and the abbreviated Pensieve reduce the audience's ability to see exactly how comprehensive and deliberate his planning was — the full picture of Dumbledore as a man who orchestrated events across years, revealing only what each person needed to know at each moment. This is a meaningful compression that slightly weakens the dramatic coherence of his posthumous agency without eliminating it. Score: 15 (role and agency recognizably reduced but intact).

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations in Deathly Hallows are the most complex and psychologically rich in the entire series. The book reveals, progressively and then fully in King's Cross, that his adult life has been shaped by: (1) guilt over Ariana's death and his own role in it — both through neglect (while absorbed in Grindelwald) and possibly through the fatal curse in the three-way duel; (2) fear of his own capacity for power, which led him to refuse the Ministry and stay at Hogwarts; (3) delayed confrontation of Grindelwald out of fear of learning which of them cast the killing curse; (4) the conflicted desire for the Deathly Hallows — specifically the Resurrection Stone, which he craved to see his dead family. His motivation for putting on the ring, despite knowing it was cursed, is explicitly stated: 'for a second I imagined that I was about to see Ariana, and my mother, and my father.' His internal conflict throughout is between his desire for power/glory (the young man who wanted to shine) and his learned self-distrust, and between his love for Harry and his willingness to use Harry as a means to an end. The line 'We have protected him because it has been essential to teach him, to raise him, to let him try his strength' — spoken coldly in the Pensieve — makes explicit that Dumbledore has instrumentalized Harry, and this creates genuine moral ambiguity around the character. His decision to withhold the full truth from Harry is motivated by calculated strategy (Harry would be tempted by the Hallows) and by self-awareness about his own weakness ('I only feared that you would fail as I had failed').
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the primary motivations adequately. In the King's Cross scene, the admission about the Hallows ('I took the Stone because I longed to recall someone who has long been at peace') is present. His guilt about Ariana is referenced directly ('You wanted to see Ariana again, didn't you, sir?' / 'Yes'). His reason for withholding the Hallows from Harry is stated clearly: 'I didn't trust you... I feared that you would make the same mistake I made.' The Pensieve scenes preserve his motivation for using Snape: strategic necessity, long-term planning, and the protection of both Harry and the school. The film also preserves the cold calculation: 'You have been raising him like a pig for slaughter' / 'But this is touching, Severus.' However, several key motivational layers are absent or underdeveloped. The film does not include Dumbledore's extended confession about his youthful selfishness — 'I was gifted, I was brilliant. I wanted to escape. I wanted to shine. I wanted glory' — which is the internal backstory that makes his adult caution and self-distrust psychologically coherent. The film also omits the scene where Dumbledore confesses he deliberately delayed confronting Grindelwald out of fear: 'I dreaded beyond all things the knowledge that it had been I who brought about her death.' Without this, the motivation for his five-year delay against Grindelwald — a key biographical fact — is absent from the film entirely. The film also cuts the passage where Dumbledore explains he refused the Ministry because he had 'proven, as a very young man, that power was my weakness.' This removes a major motivational pillar: his entire career at Hogwarts as an act of self-imposed restraint.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The immediate motivations (why he planned his death, why he withheld Hallows information, why he put on the ring) are preserved. The deeper motivational architecture — the psychology of a brilliant, self-distrusting man who shaped his entire adult life around containing his own worst impulses — is substantially underexplored in the film.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are simplified. The film gives us the conclusions of Dumbledore's self-awareness without fully showing the inner journey that produced them. Harry (and the audience) hears that Dumbledore feared his own ambition, but the specific texture — the youthful desire for glory, the fear of self-knowledge about Ariana, the deliberate avoidance of Grindelwald — is largely absent. These are not peripheral details; they are the explanatory foundation for why Dumbledore behaved as he did. The simplification is significant but does not reverse his motivations. Score: 12.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore's arc in Deathly Hallows is unusual: it is a posthumous revelation arc, unfolding through documents, memories, and the King's Cross scene. The 'arc' is not a change in present-tense behavior but a retrospective reassessment: Harry (and the reader) begins the book trusting Dumbledore implicitly, moves through growing doubt, resentment, and anger (driven by the Skeeter biography, Muriel's gossip, the lack of information, Ron's departure), reaches a nadir of disillusionment ('Let him kill me with your wand'), and then, through the Pensieve and King's Cross, arrives at a full understanding that integrates Dumbledore's flaws with genuine care and extraordinary strategic intelligence. Dumbledore's own 'arc' within the Pensieve and King's Cross is a movement from self-justification to genuine confession: he arrives at King's Cross as a man who has already accepted his failures and is ready to be honest, to ask forgiveness, and to admit that Harry is 'the better man.' The book's arc has a clear structure: Doge's obituary (idealization) → Skeeter/Muriel (doubt) → Grindelwald letter (shock) → Aberforth confrontation (challenge to trust) → Pensieve (revelation of plan) → King's Cross (integration and forgiveness). Key turning points include Harry's rage after Godric's Hollow ('Nothing was explained, nothing was given freely'), the discovery of the Grindelwald letter, Aberforth's accusations, and then Harry's decision while digging Dobby's grave to trust the Dumbledore he knew.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film largely preserves this arc but compresses the middle stages. The Doge scene at the wedding establishes early idealization; the Skeeter headlines and Muriel's revelations introduce doubt; the Grindelwald photograph is discovered in Bathilda's house and identified by Hermione; the Aberforth scene introduces the challenge to trust (though abbreviated); the Pensieve reveals the plan; King's Cross delivers the integration. Harry's emotional journey through doubt and anger is present but compressed. The film preserves the key turning points: the Grindelwald revelation, Aberforth's challenge, Harry's declaration 'I trust the man I knew,' and the King's Cross resolution. However, several important steps are either missing or reduced: (1) The extended period of Harry's resentment and bitterness while camping — during which he re-reads Skeeter's book, contemplates Dumbledore's failures with Godric's Hollow, and asks 'Had Dumbledore actually cared about Harry at all?' — is largely replaced with visual montage and tonal suggestion. (2) Harry's internal decision while digging Dobby's grave — the explicit moment where he chooses to accept Dumbledore's plan on trust — is not represented as a conscious turning point in the film. (3) The Aberforth scene in the film is substantially shorter and emotionally less developed than in the book, where Harry's response ('Because I need to. Because if I don't, I don't know who I am anymore') is more fully earned by the preceding months of doubt. (4) The King's Cross scene in the film, while well-rendered, omits Dumbledore's extended confession about his youth and the fear of Grindelwald, which is where the book's arc achieves its emotional resolution for Dumbledore himself.
character_arc.difference: The arc's shape is preserved — idealization, doubt, disillusionment, revelation, forgiveness — but several key turning points and much of the emotional texture of the middle phase (the sustained resentment, the intellectual working-through of whether to trust) are compressed or elided.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but fundamentally faithful. The film hits the major beats. The compression does cost something: the resolution in King's Cross carries less weight when the doubt phase has been shortened, and Dumbledore's own confession in King's Cross is less complete without the full confessional passages. This is a meaningful compression, not a distortion. Score: 11 (compressed but still faithful).

key_relationships.book_baseline: Dumbledore's two most important relationships in Deathly Hallows are with Harry and with Snape. His relationship with Harry is defined by a complex asymmetry: profound care combined with strategic withholding, admiration combined with instrumental use. The books show Harry oscillating between devotion and resentment precisely because Dumbledore loved him and used him simultaneously. The Pensieve reveals that Dumbledore has been raising Harry 'like a pig for slaughter' — aware Harry must die — while genuinely caring about who Harry is. In King's Cross, the relationship achieves resolution: Dumbledore asks forgiveness, Harry gives it, and the power balance shifts — Harry is now the one who comforts and defends Dumbledore ('Of course you were... how can you ask that?'). This reversal of the mentor/student hierarchy is emotionally significant. His relationship with Snape is the other major axis: cold, instrumental, and mutually dependent. Dumbledore uses Snape mercilessly ('You have been a good and faithful servant... what use would that be to anyone?' when Snape says he wishes he were dead), holds him to a terrible bargain, refuses to share information, and yet recognizes 'the best of you' in Snape's Patronus. The line 'You alone know whether it will harm your soul to help an old man avoid pain and humiliation' is both manipulative and oddly tender.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry relationship is preserved in its emotional essentials. The King's Cross scene maintains the warmth, the admission of withholding ('I didn't trust you'), and the forgiveness dynamic. However, the specific texture of Harry's resentment — the sustained anger that makes the forgiveness meaningful — is compressed in the film, as noted. The shift in power balance (Harry defending Dumbledore to himself) is present in the film but less developed. The Snape relationship is preserved in its structural outline — Dumbledore recruits him, uses him, holds him to the plan, and recognizes his love for Lily. The film Pensieve captures: 'You have been raising him like a pig for slaughter' / 'But this is touching, Severus,' the demand that Snape kill him, and the Patronus revelation. What is absent from the film: the scene where Dumbledore and Snape walk the grounds and Dumbledore manages Snape's resentment with characteristic oblique mastery; the scene where Dumbledore refuses to tell Snape why Harry needs the sword ('No, I don't think so. He will know what to do'); and the portrait's continued relationship with Snape during the war year. The emotional dynamic of the Snape relationship in the film is present but flattened: we see the outline without the full texture of Dumbledore's combination of genuine affection, deliberate opacity, and cold utility.
key_relationships.difference: Both key relationships are represented but compressed. The Harry relationship loses some of the resentment that makes the King's Cross resolution emotionally complete. The Snape relationship loses the intermediate scenes that show Dumbledore managing Snape over years — the scenes that demonstrate his habit of giving just enough trust while withholding just enough to maintain strategic advantage.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The emotional dynamics are recognizable in both relationships. The Harry relationship is mostly preserved in function and tone. The Snape relationship is more noticeably compressed: the dynamic of Dumbledore as a brilliant, affectionate, and coldly pragmatic handler of Snape is present in outline but the repeated behavioral patterns that build its texture are mostly absent. Score: 7 (mostly faithful with some compression, more notable for the Snape dynamic).

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books present a Dumbledore of extraordinary complexity. The central contradiction — the man who championed Muggle rights and became the emblem of opposition to Dark magic was, as a young man, an enthusiastic proponent of wizard supremacy — is not merely a youthful mistake but is explored with full moral seriousness. The letter to Grindelwald ('We seize control FOR THE GREATER GOOD') is given in full. Dumbledore's own confession that he 'closed his eyes' to what Grindelwald was because 'if the plans we were making came to fruition, all my dreams would come true' makes him complicit, not merely naive. The books also preserve his flaw of excessive love for plans and secrets — his habit of staging situations rather than trusting people with information, which costs him repeatedly (Snape's resentment, Harry's anguish, Ron's departure in part driven by inadequate preparation). His physical vulnerability and mortality are shown vividly in the Snape Pensieve: 'I am fortunate, extremely fortunate, that I have you, Severus' — said genuinely, not ironically. His admission that he would have made a bad Minister ('I had proven, as a very young man, that power was my weakness') is a sophisticated piece of self-knowledge that distinguishes him from a conventional wise-man archetype. The books also preserve his capacity for dark humor and emotional detachment at moments of crisis ('I confess I should prefer a quick, painless exit... Or dear Bellatrix, who likes to play with her food before she eats it').
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves several key nuances: his moral failure around the Hallows (the ring, the desire to see Ariana), his strategic instrumentalization of Harry and Snape, his admission of fear about his own judgment, and his humor in the King's Cross scene. The Pensieve sequence preserves the cold utility he applies to Snape and the specific guilt about Harry's nature as a Horcrux. However, major nuances are absent or significantly reduced: (1) The full Grindelwald ideology — Dumbledore's enthusiastic endorsement of wizard supremacy — is in the film reduced to Hermione's summary: 'He believed wizards were superior and should rule over Muggles, but gently, for their own good.' The actual letter, quoted in the books, is referenced in the film only through the signature with the Hallows symbol. The moral weight of Dumbledore having authored that ideology — 'For the Greater Good' — is substantially diminished. (2) His youth psychology — the desire to escape, to shine, the resentment of his family situation — is entirely absent from the film. (3) His five-year delay against Grindelwald driven by fear of self-knowledge is absent. (4) His capacity for dry dark humor at the expense of his own death ('death is coming for me as surely as the Chudley Cannons will finish bottom of this year's league') is absent. (5) The portrait's active wartime role — showing a Dumbledore who continues to operate even as a painted image — is absent. (6) The books establish a repeated pattern of Dumbledore making moral choices that are arguably wrong by conventional standards and doing so knowingly: raising Harry to die, using Snape's love for Lily as leverage, deliberately withholding information from both of them. The film shows these choices but frames them with less moral ambiguity — Dumbledore in King's Cross asks forgiveness and is forgiven fairly quickly, without the full weight of all he has done being articulated.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses: the full ideological depth of the Grindelwald relationship (Dumbledore as the intellectual source of 'For the Greater Good'), the youth psychology that makes his adult restraint comprehensible, the dark humor, the portrait's active agency, and the full texture of his habit of orchestrating others without their full knowledge or consent. What remains is a Dumbledore who is complex but whose complexity is somewhat summarized rather than dramatized.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is where the largest cumulative loss of book material occurs. The individual losses in other dimensions are real but manageable; taken together, they produce a film Dumbledore who is recognizably the book character but who has been simplified from a morally ambiguous, psychologically exposed, self-aware manipulator into a somewhat more straightforwardly sage-like figure whose flaws are acknowledged but not fully shown. The absence of the Grindelwald ideological material is particularly significant: in the books, this is not incidental background but the central revelation that forces Harry and the reader to hold the complexity of Dumbledore's entire public life against his private history. Score: 9 (noticeable simplification; important nuances, contradictions, and ideological depth are missing).

lost_or_transferred_material: Dumbledore's extended confessional monologue in King's Cross about his youthful desire for glory and escape from family responsibility ('I was gifted, I was brilliant. I wanted to escape. I wanted to shine. I wanted glory.')
Dumbledore's admission that he delayed confronting Grindelwald for five years because he feared learning who had cast the curse that killed Ariana
Dumbledore's explicit reasoning about why he refused to become Minister of Magic ('I had proven, as a very young man, that power was my weakness')

The full text of Dumbledore's letter to Grindelwald, which makes him the intellectual originator of 'For the Greater Good' ideology — present in the books but replaced in the film by Hermione's summary

The Pensieve scene in which Dumbledore's portrait instructs Snape on the conditions for delivering the sword ('it must be taken under conditions of need and valor — and he must not know that you give it')
The Pensieve scene in which Dumbledore refuses to tell Snape why Harry needs the sword ('No, I don't think so. He will know what to do with it')
The scene in which Dumbledore invites Snape to his office to share information, managing Snape's resentment at being kept ignorant
The extended scene in which Dumbledore explains his plan to let the Elder Wand's power die with him, including the reasoning about wand succession
The portrait of Dumbledore as an active wartime agent communicating with Snape during the year of Snape's headmastership
Dumbledore's dark humor about his own death ('death is coming for me as surely as the Chudley Cannons will finish bottom of this year's league')
The Pensieve scene where Dumbledore expresses his concern about Draco's soul ('That boy's soul is not yet so damaged')
The moment where Harry realizes what Dumbledore would have seen in the Mirror of Erised (his family alive, Ariana unharmed) — present in books through implication in King's Cross, absent from film

Aberforth's full account of Dumbledore's complicity in neglecting Ariana during the Grindelwald summer — the film version is compressed to a few lines from Aberforth without the granular detail of the books
score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (85): Applied — the films remove a significant part of Dumbledore's complexity, specifically the ideological depth of his Grindelwald relationship, his youth psychology, and the full texture of his habit of instrumentalizing people. Total does not exceed 85.
Cap 3 (75): Not strictly triggered — no major book action or decision is given to another character. Dumbledore's posthumous agency is reduced in visibility but not transferred.
Final score (72) reflects the accumulated compression across dimensions and falls below the 75 cap as appropriate given the scale of lost ideological and psychological material.
key_observations: The film portrayal of Dumbledore in Deathly Hallows is recognizably faithful at the level of broad identity, voice, and narrative function: his posthumous role as architect of the war's resolution, his warmth toward Harry, his guilt about the Hallows, and his strategic use of Snape are all present. The King's Cross and Pensieve sequences are the most faithfully rendered major scenes. However, the films lose the most psychologically dense layer of the books' Dumbledore: the young man who wanted to 'shine,' who authored the ideology behind Grindelwald's atrocities, who delayed confronting his former friend out of self-protective fear, and who managed everyone — including those he loved most — with calculated opacity. The book's Dumbledore is a man whose entire admirable adult life is a sustained act of penance for a brilliant, selfish, ideologically dangerous youth; the film's Dumbledore is a great man with acknowledged flaws. That distinction is real and consequential, producing a final score in the low 70s: faithful enough to be recognizable, simplified enough to lose what makes the character genuinely disturbing and morally complex.
